title: Story of the Youth Who Would Futter His Father's Wives (हिन्दी)

full_text:
In the city of Balkh lived an elderly and respected merchant named Khwajah Rashid, who had accumulated vast wealth through decades of honest desert commerce. His only son, Dawood, grew up pampered, headstrong, and utterly rebellious against all traditional boundaries.

On his deathbed, Khwajah Rashid summoned Dawood and gave him three final pieces of counsel:
'My son: First, never treat the honor of thy father's household with levity.
Second, never attempt to rule over those who fed and protected thee as an infant.
Third, remember that a man who sows discord within his own walls will reap ashes in the public bazaar.'

The moment the father's eyes closed in death, Dawood cast aside all solemn warnings. Filled with youthful arrogance, he sought to dispossess his father's trusted household stewards and insult the venerable matrons of the family estate, demanding absolute, humiliating obedience to his reckless whims.

The faithful chief steward, Master Kamil, warned him:
'Young master, thy father's household stands upon fifty years of mutual honor and loyalty. If thou treatest thy kin like conquered serfs, the roof will collapse upon thy head.'

Dawood struck the old steward across the face and drove him out into the night.
Deprived of the experienced stewards who managed the caravans and trade accounts, Dawood fell prey to a band of unscrupulous gamblers. Within six months, they forged debts, drained the banking vaults, and forced the sale of the ancestral mansion.

Dawood was left sitting in the dust outside the city gate in threadbare rags, begging for crusts of bread from the very porters his father had once employed.

Old Master Kamil passed by the gate, saw the ruined youth weeping in the dust, and did not mock him. He bought Dawood a bowl of hot bean soup and sat beside him:
'Dawood, thy father's words were not chains to bind thy freedom; they were the pillars that held up thy house. When a youth kicks away the foundations of respect, the fall is swift and merciless.'

Dawood wept in bitter repentance. He begged Kamil to take him as a humble apprentice in the camel stables. For seven years Dawood shoveled straw, cleaned harnesses, and learned the value of humility, slowly rebuilding an honorable life upon the bedrock of respect and honest toil.
moral: Disrespecting family honor and pursuing reckless passions brings swift disgrace; true maturity listens to wise counsel. [HI]
